mainEntity.name: What's the difference between a Roth IRA and a traditional IRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Traditional IRA contributions are often tax-deductible now but taxed on withdrawal in retirement. Roth IRA contributions are made with after-tax money now, but qualified withdrawals in retirement are completely tax-free.

mainEntity.name: Is there an income limit for contributing to a Roth IRA?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. For 2026, direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 of modified AGI for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for married couples filing jointly. Above the top of the range you can't contribute directly.

mainEntity.name: How much can I contribute to a Roth IRA in 2026?

acceptedAnswer.text: Up to $7,500, or $8,600 if you are age 50 or older by the end of the year — but never more than your taxable compensation. The limit is shared across all your traditional and Roth IRAs.

mainEntity.name: When can I withdraw Roth IRA earnings tax-free?

acceptedAnswer.text: Earnings come out tax- and penalty-free once you are 59½ and your first Roth IRA contribution was made at least five tax years earlier. Your own contributions can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty.

mainEntity.name: Do Roth IRAs have required minimum distributions?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The original owner never has to take RMDs from a Roth IRA, so the balance can keep compounding tax-free for life. Traditional IRAs require distributions starting at age 73 (75 for people born in 1960 or later).
